profile.feeling: Friendly but a little formal — the greeting for strangers and first meetings more than for close friends.

examples.text: 你好，请问地铁站在哪儿？
examples.py: Nǐ hǎo, qǐngwèn dìtiězhàn zài nǎr?
examples.tr: Hello, could you tell me where the metro station is?

collocations.tr: hello, teacher (a class to its teacher)

synonyms.nuance: the polite hello — elders, teachers, customers
hāi, ‘hi’ — borrowed from English, among young people
hālóu, ‘hello’ — playful, from English
wéi — ‘hello?’ only on the phone (and ‘hey!’ to get attention, which can be rude)

etymology.text: 你 ‘you’ + 好 ‘good, well’ — literally ‘you (are) well’.

funFacts: On the phone Chinese answer with 喂 (wéi), not with 你好.
Friends rarely say 你好 to each other: they use the name, 嗨, or a question such as 吃了吗？ ‘have you eaten?’
pitfalls: Written nǐ hǎo, spoken ní hǎo: a third tone before a third tone becomes a rising tone.
你好 is not ‘how are you?’ — the answer is simply 你好 back.
subtleties: A group is greeted with 你们好 or 大家好; a class greets its teacher with 老师好.

profile.feeling: Respectful and warm — shops, hotels, offices, elders, teachers.

examples.py: Nín hǎo, zhèli shì Zhōngguó Yínháng.
examples.tr: Hello, this is the Bank of China.

synonyms.nuance: the ordinary hello between equals
polite hello to a group or an audience

etymology.text: 您 ‘you (polite)’ + 好 ‘good, well’.

funFacts: Shop assistants greet customers with 您好，欢迎光临！ ‘Hello, welcome!’ — a set phrase you will hear everywhere.
pitfalls: There is no polite plural *您们好: to a group say 大家好 or 各位好.
Between friends 您好 sounds stiff or even ironic.
subtleties: 您 belongs above all to Beijing and northern speech; in the south and in Taiwan many people use 你好 even when being polite.

profile.feeling: Bright and polite — the morning greeting at school, at work and on the radio.

examples.py: Zǎoshang hǎo! Nǐ chī zǎofàn le ma?
examples.tr: Good morning! Have you had breakfast?

synonyms.nuance: a short ‘morning!’ between neighbours and colleagues
‘good morning’ — common in writing, messages and Taiwan
‘morning to you’ — older, northern

etymology.text: 早上 ‘morning’ + 好 ‘good’.

funFacts: 早 alone — 早！ — is the most common morning greeting among people who see each other every day.
pitfalls: Only in the morning; later in the day just say 你好.
Pronounced zǎoshang with a toneless shang.
subtleties: 早 also means ‘early’: 你来得真早！ ‘you’re really early!’

profile.feeling: A little formal — TV hosts, hotels, the start of an evening event.
profile.synonymsNone: No other set evening greeting; among friends people just say 你好 or use the name.

etymology.text: 晚上 ‘evening’ + 好 ‘good’.

funFacts: 晚 means both ‘evening’ and ‘late’ — like Spanish tarde.
pitfalls: 晚上好 greets; 晚安 says ‘good night’ when parting or going to bed.
subtleties: In everyday life 晚上好 can sound formal; friends meeting in the evening say 你好 or just the name.

profile.feeling: Soft and caring — the last word of the day, said at bedtime or at the end of a late chat.
profile.synonymsNone: No everyday alternative; 好梦 ‘sweet dreams’ is often added.

etymology.text: 晚 ‘evening, night’ + 安 ‘peace, calm’ — ‘a peaceful night’.

funFacts: Online, 晚安 wǎn’ān is sometimes playfully read as the initials of 我爱你爱你 (wǒ ài nǐ ài nǐ, ‘I love you, love you’).
pitfalls: 晚安 is for parting at night or going to bed; to greet someone in the evening say 晚上好.
Pinyin: wǎn’ān — the apostrophe shows where the syllable break is.
subtleties: In messages 晚安 often ends a late conversation, like ‘night!’ in English.

profile.feeling: The standard goodbye — neutral, correct in every situation.

examples.tr: Goodbye — take care on the way!

synonyms.nuance: ‘bye-bye’ — very common, especially on the phone and among young people
‘see you later’ — you expect to meet again soon
‘I take my leave’ — old-fashioned, formal

etymology.text: 再 ‘again’ + 见 ‘to see’: ‘see (you) again’ — Wiktionary also records the literal verb 再見 ‘to meet again’.

funFacts: The same picture as German Auf Wiedersehen, Russian до свидания, Hebrew לְהִתְרָאוֹת and Arabic إِلَى اللِّقَاء: ‘until we see / meet again’.
pitfalls: It is just ‘goodbye’ — said even when you will never meet again.
subtleties: A class says goodbye with 老师再见！, the teacher answers 同学们再见！

profile.feeling: Light and casual — friends, family, the end of a phone call.

synonyms.nuance: the neutral, always-correct goodbye

etymology.text: Phono-semantic matching of English bye-bye (拜 ‘to bow, to pay respects’).

funFacts: Phone calls often end with a quick 好，拜拜！ or even 拜拜拜拜.
pitfalls: Too casual for a boss or a teacher — use 再见 there.
Do not confuse it with the verb 拜拜 ‘to worship (the gods)’ used in Taiwan and Southeast Asia.
subtleties: Many speakers say báibái or bāibāi; dictionaries give bàibài.

override.pos: Wiktionary files 回頭見 as a “phrase”; it is a fixed parting formula, filed as INTJ like the other formulas of fd.02.

profile.feeling: Easy-going: you will meet again soon, no fixed time.

examples.py: Wǒ xiān zǒu le, huítóu jiàn!
examples.tr: I’m heading off — see you later!

synonyms.nuance: ‘see you in a bit’ — later the same day
‘see you in a while’ — the same day
‘see you tomorrow’ — any time word + 见 works: 下午见, 周一见
‘see you next time’
‘see you another day’ — no date fixed
short form of 回头见

etymology.text: 回头 ‘to turn the head; later, in a while’ + 见 ‘to see’.

funFacts: Time word + 见 is a productive pattern: 明天见 ‘see you tomorrow’, 晚上见 ‘see you tonight’, 周末见 ‘see you at the weekend’.
pitfalls: 回头见 fixes no time; for a definite meeting use time + 见 (明天见, 下午见).
subtleties: 回头 alone means ‘later’: 回头再说 ‘we’ll talk about it later’ — sometimes a polite way to put something off.

override.pos: Wiktionary files 你好嗎 as a “phrase”; it is a greeting formula, filed as INTJ like the other formulas of fd.02.

profile.feeling: A real question about someone’s wellbeing — warmer than 你好, but rarer than textbooks suggest.

examples.py: Hǎojiǔ bú jiàn, nǐ hǎo ma?
examples.tr: Long time no see — how are you?

examples.py: Nǐ hǎo ma? — Wǒ hěn hǎo, xièxie.
examples.tr: How are you? — I’m fine, thanks.

synonyms.nuance: ‘how have you been lately?’ — the natural question between friends
‘how are you doing?’
‘have you eaten?’ — a traditional greeting, not a real question about food
polite form, rare in speech

etymology.text: 你好 ‘you are well’ + the question particle 吗: ‘are you well?’

funFacts: To 吃了吗？ ‘have you eaten?’ the answer is just 吃了 or 还没 — it is a greeting, not an invitation.
pitfalls: People say 你好吗 mostly when they have not seen each other for a while; as a daily greeting it sounds like a textbook. With friends, 最近怎么样？ is more natural.
Don’t confuse it with 你好 ‘hello’, which needs no answer.
subtleties: Usual answers: 很好 (fine), 还好 / 还行 (OK), 不错 (not bad), 挺好的 (pretty good) — often followed by 你呢？ ‘and you?’

profile.feeling: Cheerful and positive — the normal answer to ‘how are you?’, and praise for good work.

senses.def: fine, well (of a person: I am fine)

examples.py: Wǒ bàba māma dōu hěn hǎo.
examples.tr: My mum and dad are both well.

synonyms.nuance: ‘not bad, pretty good’ — modest and very common
‘quite good, pretty well’
‘OK, so-so’
‘excellent’ — enthusiastic

etymology.text: 很 ‘very’ + 好 ‘good, well’. 好 is 女 ‘woman’ + 子 ‘child’; 很 first meant ‘cruel, defiant’ and became ‘very’ in the Yuan dynasty.

funFacts: 好 ‘good’ is written ‘woman’ + ‘child’.
pitfalls: No 是 before an adjective: 我很好, never *我是好 or *我是很好.
很 is often just glue: 我很好 means ‘I’m fine’, not necessarily ‘very fine’; a bare 我好 sounds like a contrast.
subtleties: Third-tone sandhi: hěn hǎo is spoken hén hǎo.
A compliment like 你的中文很好！ is answered with modesty: 哪里哪里 or 还差得远 (‘still far from it’).

override.meaning: Wiktionary: “not bad; quite OK; passable” — the course concept “fine, well (I am fine)” in its lukewarm form; the words fine/well are not in the gloss.

profile.feeling: Lukewarm: ‘OK, all right’ — not great, not bad.

senses.def: OK, all right, not bad (I am OK)
fortunately, luckily (at the start of a sentence)

synonyms.nuance: ‘OK, it’ll do’
‘so-so, average’
‘so-so’ (literally ‘horse horse tiger tiger’)
‘luckily’ — for the second sense

etymology.text: 还 hái ‘still, fairly’ + 好 ‘good, well’.

funFacts: 马马虎虎 ‘horse horse, tiger tiger’ also means ‘so-so’ — a fun synonym.
pitfalls: 还 is read hái here, not huán (‘to give back’).
Answering 还好 to 你好吗 suggests ‘nothing special’ — 很好 is the cheerful answer.
subtleties: At the start of a sentence 还好 means ‘luckily’: 还好没下雨 ‘luckily it didn’t rain’.

profile.feeling: Names and calling out: the everyday verb of introductions.

senses.def: to be called (我叫… ‘my name is …’)
to tell, to make (someone do something)

examples.text: 老师叫我们明天早点来。
examples.py: Lǎoshī jiào wǒmen míngtiān zǎo diǎn lái.
examples.tr: The teacher told us to come a bit early tomorrow.

phrases.tr: to cry bitterness to the sky

synonyms.nuance: xìng ‘to be surnamed’: 我姓王 ‘my surname is Wang’
‘to be named’ — written narration (一个名叫小明的男孩)
‘to call, to address as’ (称他为老师)
‘to shout, to call out’

etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: semantic 口 ‘mouth’ + phonetic 丩; according to the Shuowen Jiezi its original meaning was ‘to shout’.

funFacts: Chinese names put the surname first: 王小明 is Wang Xiaoming — Mr Wang. 我叫王小明 gives the whole name; 我姓王 only the surname.
pitfalls: 叫 is the verb itself — no 是: *我是叫安娜, *我叫是安娜.
To ask an older person’s name politely: 您贵姓？ ‘your honourable surname?’ — answer 我姓王.
subtleties: 我的名字是安娜 is correct too, but 我叫安娜 is the usual way.
叫 also means ‘to make, to let’: 别叫他等 ‘don’t keep him waiting’.

lexemes.pinyin: rèn shi nǐ hěn gāo xìng

profile.feeling: Friendly and polite — said once, at the first meeting.

senses.def: nice to meet you (literally ‘knowing you, I am very glad’)

examples.text: 你好，我叫安娜。——认识你很高兴！
examples.py: Nǐ hǎo, wǒ jiào Ānnà. — Rènshi nǐ hěn gāoxìng!
examples.tr: Hello, my name is Anna. — Nice to meet you!

synonyms.nuance: the same words in the other order — very common in speech
with the polite 您 — to an older or senior person
‘a pleasure to meet you’ — business and formal occasions
‘I have long admired you’ — very formal, to someone of reputation

etymology.text: 认识 ‘to know, to get acquainted with’ + 你 ‘you’ + 很高兴 ‘(I am) very glad’.
etymology.src: morphemes: 认识 + 你 + 很高兴 (Wiktionary)

funFacts: The usual reply is 我也很高兴 ‘I’m glad too’ or simply the same sentence back.
pitfalls: To someone older or senior, use 您: 认识您很高兴.
Only at the first meeting — not every time you see someone.
subtleties: Both orders are correct: 认识你很高兴 puts ‘knowing you’ first as the topic; 很高兴认识你 starts with the feeling.

lexemes.pinyin: hěn gāo xìng rèn shi nǐ

profile.feeling: Friendly and polite — the most common way to say it in conversation.

senses.def: nice to meet you (literally ‘very glad to know you’)

examples.text: 安娜，很高兴认识你，我叫小明。
examples.py: Ānnà, hěn gāoxìng rènshi nǐ, wǒ jiào Xiǎomíng.
examples.tr: Anna, nice to meet you — I’m Xiaoming.

synonyms.nuance: the same words, with ‘knowing you’ first
with the polite 您
‘a pleasure to meet you’

etymology.text: 很高兴 ‘very glad’ + 认识 ‘to get to know’ + 你 ‘you’.
etymology.src: morphemes: 很高兴 + 认识 + 你 (Wiktionary)

funFacts: 高兴 ‘glad’ is literally ‘high spirits’: 高 ‘high’ + 兴 ‘mood, interest’.
pitfalls: With a group: 很高兴认识你们; with an elder: 很高兴认识您.
subtleties: 认识 is ‘to know (a person), to be acquainted’; ‘to know a fact’ is 知道 — a split like German kennen / wissen.

profile.feeling: Grateful and polite; among family and close friends it can feel a little formal.

senses.def: to thank (verb: 谢谢你的帮助)

synonyms.nuance: ‘many thanks’
‘thanks’ — casual, quick
‘to thank; gratitude’ — speeches, letters (非常感谢 ‘thank you very much’)

etymology.text: Reduplication of 谢 ‘to thank’ (言 ‘speech’ + phonetic 射).

funFacts: Polite refusal is part of the ritual: offered food or a gift, many people decline once or twice before accepting.
pitfalls: The second 谢 is toneless: xièxie.
Thanking close family for small things can sound distant or ironic.
subtleties: To decline: 不用了，谢谢 ‘no, thanks’; to reply to thanks: 不客气.

profile.feeling: Kind and modest: ‘no need to be so polite’.

senses.def: impolite, blunt (in other contexts: 说话很不客气)

examples.text: 不客气，这是我应该做的。
examples.py: Bú kèqi, zhè shì wǒ yīnggāi zuò de.
examples.tr: You’re welcome — it was the least I could do.

synonyms.nuance: ‘no need to thank (me)’
‘no problem’
‘it’s nothing’ — for a small favour or gift

etymology.text: 不 ‘not’ + 客气 ‘polite, standing on ceremony’: ‘don’t be so polite’.

funFacts: 别客气 ‘don’t be polite’ is also what a host says when offering food: help yourself!
pitfalls: 不客气 answers 谢谢; to 对不起 the answer is 没关系 ‘never mind’.
不 is said bú here, because 客 kè has the 4th tone.
subtleties: In other sentences 不客气 means ‘rude, blunt’: 他对我很不客气 ‘he was rude to me’.

profile.feeling: Courteous and inviting — the word that opens doors: 请进, 请坐.

senses.def: please (before a verb: 请坐 ‘please sit down’)
to invite; to treat (to a meal)
to ask, to request (someone to do something)

examples.tr: Today I’m treating you to a meal.
We ask the teacher for help.

collocations.tr: to treat, to pay for others

phrases.tr: invite the gentleman into the urn
phrases.meaning: to trap someone with his own scheme

synonyms.nuance: ‘may I trouble you’: 麻烦你帮我一下 — the usual way to ask a favour
polite northern ‘excuse me, would you mind’
‘kindly …’ — written notices
‘to invite’ — invitations, events

etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: semantic 言 ‘speech’ + phonetic 青.

funFacts: Whoever says 我请客 ‘I’m inviting’ pays the bill — and friends sometimes argue over who gets to.
pitfalls: 请 goes before the verb: 请坐 — never at the end like English ‘…, please’.
For a favour 请 alone can sound stiff; 麻烦你… or 能不能… is more natural.
subtleties: On its own, 请！ or 您请！ with a gesture means ‘after you / go ahead / help yourself’.
On signs, 请勿 means ‘please do not’: 请勿吸烟 ‘no smoking’.

profile.feeling: A real apology — sincere, for something that matters.

synonyms.nuance: a lighter ‘sorry, excuse me’ — for small things
‘I’m sorry, I apologize’ — written and formal speech (很抱歉)
‘please forgive me’

etymology.text: 对 ‘to face, to treat’ + 不起 ‘not up to it’ (as in 买不起 ‘can’t afford’): ‘I can’t face you — I have let you down’.
etymology.src: morphemes: 对 + 不起 (Wiktionary: 對不起 “to let down”)

funFacts: The reply is 没关系 ‘it doesn’t matter’ — literally ‘no connection’.
pitfalls: For a small slip — bumping into someone, interrupting — 不好意思 is more natural than 对不起.
Pronounced duìbuqǐ, with a toneless bu.
subtleties: As a verb: 我对不起他 ‘I wronged him’ — the opposite is 对得起 ‘to be worthy of, not let down’.

profile.feeling: Light and everyday: ‘sorry, excuse me’ — a little embarrassed smile in words.

examples.text: 不好意思，请问洗手间在哪儿？
examples.py: Bù hǎoyìsi, qǐngwèn xǐshǒujiān zài nǎr?
examples.tr: Excuse me, where is the toilet?
Sorry, could you let me through?

synonyms.nuance: a real apology
‘sorry to bother you’

etymology.text: 不 ‘not’ + 好意思 ‘to feel at ease, to have the nerve’: ‘I feel embarrassed’.

funFacts: It is probably the most used ‘sorry’ in daily life — waiters, strangers, colleagues all use it.
pitfalls: Not for serious wrongs: there you need 对不起.
subtleties: Also softens a refusal or request: 不好意思，我明天不能来 ‘sorry, I can’t come tomorrow’.

profile.feeling: Polite and considerate — interrupting someone or getting their attention.

senses.def: excuse me (to interrupt or get attention)

examples.text: 打扰一下，请问地铁站在哪儿？
examples.py: Dǎrǎo yíxià, qǐngwèn dìtiězhàn zài nǎr?
examples.tr: Excuse me, where is the metro station?

examples.py: Dǎrǎo yíxià, zhèli yǒu rén ma?
examples.tr: Excuse me, is this seat taken?

collocations.tr: sorry to have bothered you (when leaving)

synonyms.nuance: the most common way to get a stranger’s attention
‘may I ask’ — right before a question
polite northern ‘excuse me’, also to get past
‘let me pass’ — in a crowd

etymology.text: 打扰 ‘to disturb’ + 一下 ‘a moment, a bit’: ‘let me disturb you for a moment’.

funFacts: Leaving after a visit, 打扰了 ‘I have disturbed (you)’ is a polite goodbye.
pitfalls: It is for interrupting or asking; to get past people say 借过, 让一下 or 劳驾.
一 changes tone before the 4th tone: yí xià.
subtleties: Often combined: 不好意思，打扰一下，请问… — three polite openers in a row are normal.

override.pos: Wiktionary files 勞駕 as a verb (“(polite, dated) excuse me; may I trouble you?”); it is used as a fixed polite formula, filed as INTJ like the other formulas of fd.02.

profile.feeling: Old-Beijing courtesy — polite, slightly old-fashioned.

senses.def: excuse me; may I trouble you (to ask a favour or to get past)

examples.tr: Excuse me, excuse me, let me through.

examples.py: Láojià, nín bāng wǒ kàn yíxià.
examples.tr: Would you mind having a look for me?

synonyms.nuance: the usual ‘excuse me’ when interrupting
‘may I trouble you’ — the everyday way to ask a favour
‘excuse me, let me pass’

etymology.text: 劳 ‘to trouble, to make toil’ + 驾 ‘carriage’, an honorific for the other person (as in 大驾 ‘your honour’): ‘trouble your carriage’.
etymology.src: morphemes: 劳 + 驾 (Wiktionary: 勞駕 “(polite, dated) excuse me; may I trouble you?”)

funFacts: 劳驾 belongs to the courteous speech of old Beijing; you will hear it from older people and in films.
pitfalls: Mostly northern and a little dated; younger speakers say 不好意思 or 麻烦你.
subtleties: It works both for asking a favour and for asking people to step aside.

override.meaning: Wiktionary: 對 “correct; true; right”; its use as an answer meaning ‘yes, that’s right’ is the course concept “yes”, which the gloss does not word.

profile.feeling: Agreement: ‘right, exactly’ — the most common way to say yes to a statement.

senses.def: right, correct; (as an answer) yes, that’s right
towards, to (before a person: 他对我很好)
a pair (measure word: 一对夫妻 ‘a couple’)

examples.tr: He is very good to me.

phrases.tr: the doors match, the houses match
phrases.meaning: a well-matched marriage (families of equal standing)

phrases.tr: to play the lute to a cow
phrases.meaning: to talk to someone who cannot understand; to cast pearls before swine

synonyms.nuance: ‘yes, it is’ — to questions with 是
a soft, common ‘yes, that’s right’
‘mm-hm’
‘exactly, no mistake’
‘correct’ — answers in exams, official texts

etymology.text: In the oracle-bone and bronze scripts an ideogrammic compound: 丵 (a digging tool) + 土 ‘earth’ + 又 ‘hand’; the character was later borrowed for ‘to reply’.

funFacts: Chinese has no all-purpose ‘yes’: people repeat the verb (要。是。有。) or say 对 ‘right’ to confirm a statement.
对了！ is the classic ‘oh, by the way!’ that changes the topic.
pitfalls: 对 confirms that something is right; to accept an offer (你要吗？) answer 要, not 对.
subtleties: 对对对, said three times quickly, is a typical eager agreement.

profile.feeling: Short, clear refusal or denial — the everyday ‘not’.

senses.def: not (negates verbs, adjectives and 是: habits, wishes, the present and the future)
cannot (between a verb and its complement: 听不懂)

phrases.meaning: see you there — I’ll wait until you come

synonyms.nuance: negates 有 and says that something did not happen
bié: ‘don’t!’ in commands
‘not, is not’ in written style (非卖品 ‘not for sale’)

etymology.text: Originally a pictogram of the calyx of a flower; borrowed for the negation. A new character 柎 was later made for ‘calyx’.

funFacts: The textbook says 不 (bù) has 4th tone, yet you will hear it as bú almost as often — before every 4th-tone syllable.
pitfalls: Tone sandhi: before a 4th tone 不 is said bú — 不是 bú shì, 不要 bú yào; in 听不懂 and A-not-A questions it is toneless.
Never 不有 — the negation of 有 is 没有.
For a past event use 没: 我昨天没去, not *我昨天不去.
subtleties: 不 can express will: 我不去 ‘I won’t go / I refuse to go’.
As an answer, Chinese prefers to repeat the verb: 你要吗？— 不要。 A bare 不 sounds blunt.
